analysis.one_liner: Requires a seven-day waiting period and law enforcement background check before handgun sales.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Judiciary Committee and died without a vote when the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for licensed gun dealers to hand over a handgun until either seven days pass with no objection from local law enforcement, or the buyer already has a verified permit or an equivalent state check. Buyers must fill out a form stating they have no felony record, are not fugitives, and are not otherwise barred from owning guns; police must destroy the paperwork within 30 days unless a sale is blocked. The bill also sends federal grant money to states to computerize criminal records and pay for running the checks.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities affected by handgun violence gain a cooling-off period and a records check that keeps handguns away from convicted felons, fugitives, and others legally barred from buying them. Local police departments gain federal grants to computerize criminal records and cover the cost of doing the checks. Ordinary buyers get a clear, privacy-protected process: their statements are destroyed within 30 days, and officers are shielded from lawsuits for doing the check.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Handgun violence victims and law-abiding buyers

how_it_helps.text: Licensed dealers may not transfer a handgun for seven days after the buyer applies, giving local law enforcement time to check whether the buyer is barred by law from possessing it [S3][S2].

Buyers must swear they are not under felony indictment or conviction, not fugitives, not unlawful drug users, not adjudicated mentally defective or committed to a mental institution, not illegally present aliens, not dishonorably discharged, and not citizenship renouncers [S3][S2].

The bill allows faster alternatives for buyers who already have a state-verified permit or a documented threat to their life or household, so the delay does not block people in immediate danger [S3][S2].
Police must destroy the buyer's statement and related records within 30 days unless the sale would violate law, and officers get immunity from liability for running the check [S3][S2].
The Attorney General would grant states up to $40 million a year to computerize criminal history records and defray the cost of conducting the background checks [S3][S2].

analysis.who_pays: Licensed handgun dealers bear new paperwork, a mandatory waiting period, and the risk of fines up to $1,000 or one year in prison for violations; some sales are delayed or lost. State and local law enforcement agencies take on the work of checking each buyer, though federal grants are meant to defray those costs. Buyers who want a handgun right away wait at least seven days.
analysis.who_pays_short: Licensed handgun dealers and some buyers

drawbacks.text: The seven-day wait delays every purchase from a licensed dealer, including by law-abiding buyers; the bill carves out faster paths for permit holders and people facing documented threats, but most buyers simply wait [S3].

State and local police must perform the checks with whatever records are available, and the bill's own grant program exists because many states' criminal records were not computerized enough to make the checks reliable [S3].
The check applies only to sales by licensed dealers, so it cannot reach private or unlicensed transfers — the same limit that later shaped debates over the final law's scope [S3].
The bill authorizes but does not guarantee the $40 million in annual grants; without appropriations, local agencies absorb the cost of checks and records improvements themselves [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is a one-week delay and modest paperwork for dealers and police against a filter that keeps handguns from people already barred by law. The bill tries to blunt the main objections: privacy (records destroyed in 30 days), speed for people in danger (threat and permit exceptions), and local cost (federal grants, officer liability protection). Its weak spot is reliance on state criminal records that were often incomplete in 1991 — a weakness the bill acknowledges with its own grants program rather than solves.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, sent to its Constitution Subcommittee in July 1991, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Senator George Mitchell of Maine introduced the bill on June 11, 1991, joined by Senators Kohl and Gore [S1][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day [S5].
On July 29, 1991, it was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on the Constitution [S5].
No further action was recorded; the bill never reached the Senate floor and expired when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Licensed handgun dealers and opponents of waiting periods were better off, because the bill died without ever coming to a vote.

for.name: George J. Mitchell
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-ME), bill sponsor and Senate Majority Leader
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act on June 11, 1991.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee and its Constitution Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and sent it to the Constitution Subcommittee on July 29, 1991; no markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever followed.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Led public and lobbying opposition to mandatory waiting periods and background checks during the early-1990s Brady debates.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only three Democratic sponsors and no Republican cosponsors, but the bill never reached a vote, so no roll calls reveal how the parties would have split.

industries.note: The bill forces licensed sellers to wait seven days, collect sworn statements, and check with local police before every handgun sale, with fines up to $1,000 and one year in prison for violations. The industry's interest in unrestricted, immediate sales ran against the bill's purpose of screening out prohibited buyers.

industries.industry: State and local law enforcement agencies
industries.note: Police take on the work of checking every buyer against criminal records, but the bill pays for it with federal grants, shields officers from liability, and funds computerized record systems that improve their own case data.
